scams.name: The Pedicab Meter Manipulation
scams.tldr: He does not mention the rate.
scams.description:
He does not mention the rate. You hop in and enjoy the ten-minute ride through the charming streets. When you arrive, he points to a small meter and announces you owe $60. The rate is $1.50 per minute, and he took the longest possible route, stopped multiple times to "call in" for directions, and chatted with friends along the way — all while the meter ran.

Travelers warn repeatedly about pedicab overcharges in Key West, reporting that the same nine-block ride cost anywhere from $7.50 to $30 depending on the driver's route and stops. The Key West Travel Guide specifically advises tourists to always agree on a price before beginning a pedicab journey and to ride only with drivers who will state the price upfront. The pattern is consistent: drivers pretend not to know where destinations are located and stop repeatedly to "call in" while the per-minute meter keeps running.
scams.avoidance: Always ask "What is the total fare to my destination?" before getting in any pedicab, and ride only with drivers who give you a flat rate. Agree on the price in advance and get verbal confirmation — do not accept "we'll see" or per-minute pricing. Most of Old Town Key West is walkable, so consider walking rather than taking a pedicab for distances under a mile. Use the free Duval Loop bus service that runs a continuous route through Old Town. If a price dispute arises, note the driver's name and pedicab number and report it to the Key West Code Compliance office.
scams.location: Duval Street, Mallory Square, throughout Old Town Key West, and routes between cruise ship port and attractions

scams.name: The Cosmetics Shop High-Pressure Scam
scams.tldr: You are strolling down Duval Street when an attractive young salesperson steps in front of you offering a free skin-care sample.
scams.description:
You are strolling down Duval Street when an attractive young salesperson steps in front of you offering a free skin-care sample. They rub cream on your hand and usher you inside. The compliments flow: your skin is beautiful, this product will make you look ten years younger. Before you know it, you are being shown products with price tags in the hundreds or thousands of dollars, told you are getting an incredible one-time deal. One visitor reported that the company charged her credit card $958.90 for two purchases and then never sent the promised products.

This scam grew so pervasive that a citizen group called the Key West Rip-Off Rapid Response Team waged a five-year battle against these cosmetic shops. The Oro Gold shop at 518 Duval Street was suspended for ten days for repeated code violations before being allowed to reopen, and the Rip-Off Team picketed outside the store. The city of Key West eventually took aim at the predatory sales practices, and the controversy escalated to include violence and ugly public accusations. Many tourists have come forward with accounts of credit card fraud after being overcharged and never receiving their products.
scams.avoidance: Do not stop for anyone offering free samples on Duval Street — a firm "No thanks" while you keep walking is enough. Never give your credit card to a salesperson in a high-pressure environment without carefully reading what you are signing. If you accidentally engage, say "I need to think about it" and leave — there is no deal that expires the moment you walk out. Check online reviews of any cosmetics shop on Duval Street before purchasing anything. If you believe you were scammed, contact the Key West Code Compliance office and dispute the charge with your credit card company immediately.
scams.location: Duval Street, particularly around 518 Duval Street and other Dead Sea cosmetics shops in the downtown area

scams.name: The Parking and Towing Trap
scams.tldr: The signage is confusing — some tow zone signs sit on private property but appear to apply to the public street, while other signs mark what looks like a public road but is actually a private street.
scams.description:
The signage is confusing — some tow zone signs sit on private property but appear to apply to the public street, while other signs mark what looks like a public road but is actually a private street. You come back an hour later and your car is gone. The tow costs $135 by city ordinance for the basic charge, but unadvertised fees for storage, mileage, and after-hours recovery push the real total to $350 to $400 or more.

Visitors describe the confusing signage and unexpectedly high tow fees in detail. Tow zone signs do not post all the fees, and some private property signs are positioned to appear as though they apply to adjacent public street parking. Parking enforcement runs daily from 8 a.m. to midnight, and first-time visitors are better off using metered lots than street parking. The city has also cracked down on handicap parking fraud, in which tourists borrow placards to park free in premium downtown spots.
scams.avoidance: Use the official city parking garage at the corner of Grinnell and Caroline Streets rather than searching for street parking. If you must park on the street, photograph all signs near your vehicle and note the meter expiration time. Pay for parking using the ParkMobile app, which sends expiration reminders to your phone. Consider leaving your car at your hotel and using the free Duval Loop bus or renting a bicycle to explore Old Town. Read the fine print on every sign near your parking spot — if any sign is confusing or seems to apply to your spot, move your car.
scams.location: Throughout Old Town Key West, private lots disguised as public parking, streets near Duval and the cruise ship port

scams.name: The Sunset Sail Bait and Switch
scams.tldr: You see a flyer advertising a romantic sunset sail for $45 per person with "open bar, live music, and hors d'oeuvres." You book it.
scams.description:
You see a flyer advertising a romantic sunset sail for $45 per person with "open bar, live music, and hors d'oeuvres." You book it. You board the catamaran and discover 120 other tourists packed onto the deck. The "open bar" is cheap well liquor and one type of wine. The "hors d'oeuvres" are crackers and cheese. The "live music" is a speaker playing Jimmy Buffett songs. Meanwhile, a premium sailboat with twenty guests sails past with champagne and a real musician for $95 per person — the experience you thought you were getting.

While not technically a scam, the gap between what is advertised and what is delivered on budget sunset cruises is one of the most common complaints in Key West. Travelers describe overcrowded catamarans where you cannot even see the sunset from your position, drinks limited to a single type of cheap rum punch, and disappointingly minimal food. Compare operators carefully and read recent reviews rather than relying on marketing photos, which typically show the boat with a handful of photogenic guests rather than the 100-plus reality.
scams.avoidance: Read the most recent reviews before booking any sunset cruise, and pay attention to comments about crowding and drink quality. Ask specifically how many guests will be on board — smaller boats with 20 to 30 guests provide a vastly better experience. Book directly with the operator rather than through street kiosks or hotel concierge desks that earn commissions for filling cheap tours. If an "open bar" is advertised, ask what specific drinks are included before booking. Consider spending more for a smaller catamaran or schooner sail — the difference in experience is worth the extra cost.
scams.location: Key West Harbor, charter boat docks along the waterfront, and ticket kiosks near Mallory Square

scams.name: Duval Street Bar Overpouring and Tab Padding
scams.tldr: You sit down at a busy Duval Street bar and the bartender is incredibly generous, pouring enormous drinks and offering free shots.
scams.description:
You sit down at a busy Duval Street bar and the bartender is incredibly generous, pouring enormous drinks and offering free shots. The tab grows quickly. By the third round, the drinks are so strong you are not keeping close track. At the end of the night, your credit card is charged for drinks you do not remember ordering, shots that were "on the house" that somehow appeared on the bill, and a gratuity that was automatically added at 20 to 25 percent on top of already inflated prices. Some tourists wake up the next morning to find that their card was charged multiple times.

Tourists report credit card charges far exceeding what they believed they spent, particularly at bars where tabs were left open. Key West's open-container laws, which allow you to walk the streets with a drink, contribute to a party atmosphere where tourists lose track of their spending. Some bars charge $15 to $18 for standard cocktails that would cost $8 to $10 elsewhere in Florida, and the tab padding is harder to detect after several rounds of strong drinks.
scams.avoidance: Pay for each round individually in cash rather than running an open tab whenever possible. Ask for prices before ordering — cocktail prices on Duval Street can vary dramatically from bar to bar. Review your receipt carefully before signing, and count the number of items against what you actually ordered. Set a spending limit for the evening and switch to water or leave when you reach it. Take a photo of your receipt before leaving so you can dispute charges later if necessary.
scams.location: Bars along Duval Street, particularly open-air bars near the 400-600 blocks, and establishments near the cruise ship port

scams.name: The Vacation Rental Listing Fraud
scams.tldr: A charming cottage with a pool, just blocks from Duval Street, is offered at an unbelievably good weekly rate.
scams.description:
A charming cottage with a pool, just blocks from Duval Street, is offered at an unbelievably good weekly rate. You wire the deposit and arrive to find that the address belongs to someone else who has no idea their property was listed. The scammer stole photos and descriptions from legitimate rental sites, created a fake listing, collected your deposit, and vanished.

Thieves steal photos and descriptions from real properties and place bogus ads on third-party sites. Visitors report paying deposits for properties that either do not exist or belong to people who never authorized the listing, and the problem stretches across the entire island chain of the Florida Keys.
scams.avoidance: Book through established platforms like Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com that offer payment protection and verified listings. Never wire money directly to a property owner — use only platform-based payment systems. Search the property address on Google Maps Street View to confirm the building exists and matches the photos. Read reviews from previous guests and check that the property has a consistent review history. If a deal seems too good to be true for Key West, especially during high season, it almost certainly is.
scams.location: Online listings for properties throughout Key West, particularly on third-party rental sites and social media
